export const GENERIC_BOT_RE = /bot\b|bot\/|bot;|crawl|spider|slurp|scanner|fetcher|preview|monitor|checker|archiver|indexer|\+https?:\/\//i;

export function matchCrawler(ua: string): CrawlerDef | null {
  for (const c of CRAWLERS) if (c.re.test(ua)) return c;
  return null;
}

export function matchAutomation(ua: string): string | null {
  for (const a of AUTOMATION) if (a.re.test(ua)) return a.id;
  return null;
}

export function crawlerById(id: string): CrawlerDef | undefined {
  return CRAWLERS.find((c) => c.id === id);
}

export function crawlerLabel(id: string): string {
  if (id === "other-bot") return "Other declared bot";
  if (id.startsWith("auto:")) return `Automation (${id.slice(5)})`;
  return crawlerById(id)?.label ?? id;
}

I should check whether tsconfig has resolveJsonModule enabled, then start on a pure classification function that takes in the UA, IP, path, referrer, user ID, webdriver flag, and any known crawler verification status. I'm working out the logic: flag as a scraper if there's no UA, and if a crawler pattern matches, check whether its definition requires verification via reverse DNS or IP list lookup.

If verification confirms a match, mark it a verified crawler; if it fails, flag it as a spoofed scraper; if verification status is unknown, mark it a declared, unverified crawler pending async checks later. I'm also laying out rules for automation tool matches (scraper), generic bot matches (declared-crawler), webdriver detection (suspected-bot), flagged IPs, and a weak-signal scoring system combining stale browser versions, datacenter IPs, malformed UAs, and missing OS/browser parsing, where signed-in users get leniency unless strong signals are present and a score of 3+ triggers a suspected-bot verdict, otherwise defaulting to human. Now I'm figuring out how to estimate current browser major versions over time for Chrome and Firefox based on their release cadence, so I can flag stale browser signatures.

I'm settling on a 24-month-behind threshold for flagging stale browsers, weighted heavily (3 points) since it's rare but meaningful, while accounting for edge cases like Chrome's Android UA freeze and legitimate old Windows 7 stragglers. I'm also starting to design an async worker for behavioral re-classification, including velocity checks (excessive pageviews per IP in short windows triggering scraper flags) and beginning session-based signals.

I'll drop no-interaction as a standalone signal since it's too weak alone, instead folding it into ua-cluster as a dampener (clusters with over 20% interaction rate get excluded). For honeypot, I'll flag the IP directly and mark all its visits in the last 24h as scraper via the route handler.

Then the reclassification step writes isBot/botKind/botReason/botCheckedAt back to Visit records, and also sweeps unclassified rows in batches to backfill historical data.

The worker should keep its re-classification window limited to the last 48h rather than touching full history, so any full backfill stays a deliberate owner-run script rather than automatic. On precedence, the async process should only ever upgrade verdicts (human→suspected/scraper, declared→verified/scraper) and never downgrade a stronger ingest-time verdict. For verification, I'll have it run cached FCrDNS lookups on declared-crawler rows marked "unverified," capped at 20 per sweep.

For verification, I should dedupe by (bot, ip) pairs per sweep and cap unverified lookups around 50, treating unknowns as still "declared-crawler" until resolved -- major bots like Google/Bing/Apple/OpenAI can skip DNS entirely since they publish IP lists, while something like Amazonbot needs rDNS lookups across many IPs, so caching matters a lot there. Now I'm moving on to scope.ts, where I need to read a "nx_inc_bots" cookie via next/headers to control the include-bots toggle, then pull together the classify, verify, ip-flags, and scope pieces.

Given the small dataset sizes, in-memory aggregation should work fine everywhere, though I'll keep queries bounded and use the isBot+createdAt index for the larger visit table. I'm planning to write one insights module per tab, and need to check server statuses for active paid accounts along with hosting and email subscription details.

For MRR, I should stay consistent with the admin dashboard's fleetMrrCents calculation and reuse the withAccounts select shape from analytics.ts as a shared constant. For churn, I'll combine ServerArchive data with live servers, defining a paying customer as one with a non-free server active at a given time, counting RUNNING/STOPPED/SUSPENDED/REINSTALLING as active but excluding PENDING/ERROR. Customer churn would compare paying customers at period start versus period end, normalized to a monthly rate, while revenue churn for archived servers isn't feasible since pricing data is missing—so I'll stick to logo churn only to keep things honest.

For retention, I'm leaning toward first-payment cohorts tracked by server lifetimes rather than calendar-month revenue cohorts, since that's more meaningful for a hosting business—each cohort cell shows the percentage of users still holding an active paid server k months after their first payment. For LTV, I'll compute both realized (average and median net spend per paying customer) and a simple predicted estimate using ARPU divided by monthly churn, clearly labeled as a rough formula. I'm also sketching a churn-risk list that flags paying customers with warning signs like autoRenew disabled on a soon-expiring server, active dunning, or no portal activity combined with a stopped server.

Now I'm planning out the funnel metrics: bot-filtered visitors, signups, deployed users, and paid users, each compared against the previous period, plus time-to-first-deploy and time-to-first-payment percentiles. I also want to break conversion down by acquisition source, partner, and country—pulling country from either billing info or the user's earliest bot-free visit—and separately track conversion from free Minecraft server signups into paying customers.

I'm also mapping out a products view grouped by game family or VPS plan, computing MRR and committed RAM per group, then allocating node hosting costs proportionally by committed RAM share to estimate margin per product line, flagging nodes with unknown costs, and tracking new orders per group versus the prior period before moving into node capacity planning.

For capacity, I'm pulling committed RAM from deployed servers on each node, actual used RAM from recent memory samples, computing utilization, and deriving growth trends from historical snapshots or reconstructing them from server creation and deletion events over the last 60 days against each node's RAM ceiling.

#!/bin/bash
# Global lock so only ONE heavy job (tsc, next dev, playwright, test suites) runs at a time on
# this box. This machine is the live production primary (also hosts ~40 customer VMs, swap is
# nearly full) — uncontrolled parallel tsc/dev servers can OOM or starve production.
# usage: heavy.sh bash -c "cd /opt/nxeon-wt-foo && npx tsc --noEmit -p ."
exec flock -w 3600 /tmp/nxeon-heavy.lock nice -n 19 ionice -c3 env NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=3072" "$@"

## Admin surfaces

40+ sections, grouped by `lib/admin-groups.ts:44-211` into five nav sections with sub-tabs
(`components/admin/SubTabs.tsx:61`). Every legacy `/admin/*` route remains reachable.

| Group | Sections |
|---|---|
| Overview | `/admin` dashboard, `/admin/analytics`, `/admin/visitors` |
| Clients | `/admin/users`, `/admin/users/[id]`, `/admin/orgs`, `/admin/grant` |
| Support | `/admin/support`, `/admin/chat`, `/admin/feedback` |
| Fleet | `/admin/servers`, `/admin/nodes`, `/admin/ips`, `/admin/provisioning`, `/admin/jobs`, `/admin/monitoring`, `/admin/abuse`, `/admin/infrastructure` |
| Billing | `/admin/billing`, `/admin/invoices`, `/admin/subscriptions`, `/admin/plans`, `/admin/products`, `/admin/coupons`, `/admin/gift-codes`, `/admin/game-plans`, `/admin/email-plans`, `/admin/affiliate` |
| Platform | `/admin/settings`, `/admin/staff`, `/admin/audit`, `/admin/logs`, `/admin/automation`, `/admin/improvements`, `/admin/email-templates`, `/admin/mail`, `/admin/domains`, `/admin/games`, `/admin/blog`, `/admin/newsletter`, `/admin/testimonials`, `/admin/docs` |

**The four you will use most when something is wrong:**

| Page | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| `/admin/jobs` | Every `Job` with `type`, `status`, `attempts`, `step`, `error`. First stop for anything that "did nothing". |
| `/admin/servers/[id]` | The full row: status, `suspendReason`, `dunningStage`, `expiresAt`, `extraDiskGB`, volumes, jobs. |
| `/admin/logs` | The `EmailLog` — what was actually sent, to whom, and whether it errored. |
| `/admin/audit` | `AuditLog` — every privileged action, including impersonated ones attributed to the real admin. |

**Impersonation.** `impersonateUser()` sets a signed cookie; `currentUser()` returns the target and
`realUser()` the actual admin. A banner and exit control are handled in
`components/portal/Shell.tsx`. Admin pages call `realUser`/`requireArea` and **refuse to render while
impersonating**. Every money-spending action is blocked while impersonating —
`lib/actions.ts:235`, `:382`, `:491`, `:591`, `lib/actions-disk.ts:41`,
`lib/actions-domains-transfer.ts:133`, `lib/actions-2fa.ts:78`.

**Honest notes.** There is **no `/admin/backups`** page, despite the backup scripts writing status JSON
for one. There is **no admin migration surface at all** — `db.migration` is referenced only in
`lib/actions-migrate.ts`. And `worker/index.ts:229`/`:476` read a setting **`dedicated_ip_default`**
that is not in `SETTINGS_DEFAULTS` and appears in no panel — a provisioning-behaviour knob no admin can
see or set, silently defaulting to `true`. That is the inverse of the saved-but-unread defect: read but
unsettable.

  dedicated-IP branch now reads `server.guestSshPort ?? 22` instead of a bare `22`. Selected into

  would still fail — this guest's `iptables` (legacy) returns "Incompatible with this kernel" (likely
  1Panel's own nftables-only setup). Checked the LIVE guest directly: `iptables -L INPUT` showed only
  UFW's own chains (`ufw-before-input` etc.), policy DROP — confirming the platform's `NXEON_FW` chain
  has in fact never once been successfully applied to this guest, so there was nothing live to
  "detach". The customer's 6 stale `FirewallRule` DB rows are display-only leftovers; deleting them
  requires no guest-side sync (and syncing them now would risk appending a default-DROP that doesn't

  a sync). `SYNC_FIREWALL` jobs are only ever created by `lib/actions-firewall.ts` on an explicit rule
  edit (confirmed — no periodic/cron trigger exists), so once those 6 rows are gone, nothing re-fires
  on its own.

  Worth a platform-wide follow-up too: any guest running an nftables-only setup (1Panel defaults to
  this) can never successfully use the panel firewall feature at all, independent of this port issue.

# Admin Insights — proposals beyond the first build (2026-10-01)

`/admin/insights` shipped with: revenue/MRR/ARR, churn + paying-customer cohorts + LTV,
the bot-free signup→deploy→paid funnel with time-to-first-deploy/payment and conversion by
source/partner/country, free-MC→paid, per-game/per-plan popularity and RAM-allocated margin,
per-node capacity + days-until-full, job failure rate and latency, support load and response
times, partner/creator performance, email open/click by template, payment failures/dunning,
refunds/chargebacks, and crawler/SEO stats from the nginx access log. Every number is a DB
query; anything without enough data says so.

This file ranks what is worth building NEXT, by value to this business (a small, owner-run VPS +
game-hosting company where one churned customer is a visible dent and one full node blocks
sales) against effort in this codebase. **Implemented** items are marked.

| # | Feature | Value | Effort | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Low-capacity forecast alerts** — per node, days until committed RAM hits capacity at the current growth rate; WARN ≤30d / CRITICAL ≤14d or 85% / 95% committed | Very high: a full node silently blocks every new order on it | S | **Implemented** — `lib/insights/alerts.ts` `capacityAlerts`, evaluated hourly by `worker/insights.ts` into `InsightsAlert`, auto-resolves |
| 2 | **Revenue / payment anomaly alerts** — yesterday's earned revenue and cash vs a 28-day baseline (z ≤ −2.5), refund spikes (>3× and >$50), payment-failure-email spikes | Very high: a broken Stripe key or renewal sweep shows up as "revenue quietly stopped" days later | S | **Implemented** — `revenueAlerts`; only fires once a real baseline exists (≥$5/day average over ≥10 non-zero days) |
| 3 | **Churn-risk list** — paying customers scored on concrete signals (auto-renew off near expiry, dunning, payment-failure emails, every server stopped 14d+, no portal visit 30d, ticket waiting on staff >24h) | High: it is a call list; saving one $20/mo customer pays for the feature | S | **Implemented** — `churnRiskList`, shown on Overview (top 5) and Churn & LTV (top 30), exported in CSV |
| 4 | **Stripe dispute webhook** (`charge.dispute.created/closed`) → a `Dispute` table, auto-reversing partner commission, and real chargeback rate on Payments | High: today chargebacks only exist if an admin types one in; the processor can drop an account for a rate we can't see | M | Proposed — needs a webhook-secret-gated handler in `app/api/stripe/webhook` (Stripe owner area) |
| 5 | **`Job.startedAt` / `finishedAt`** columns stamped by the worker | High for ops: lets Jobs split queue wait from run time (today it honestly shows end-to-end only); also what D1's job metrics need | S | Proposed — owned by the worker-loop agent (D1); `lib/insights/ops.ts` already detects the columns at runtime and switches automatically |
| 6 | **Weekly owner digest** — a Monday summary (MRR delta, churned + new paying, open alerts, top churn risks, crawler errors) delivered to the owner's own inbox only | Medium-high: puts the page in front of the owner without them opening it | S | Proposed — must use the existing mailer with a fixed internal recipient; never customers |
| 7 | **Revenue by product line over time** — earned revenue split VPS / game / hosting / email / domains | Medium: the wallet ledger has no `kind` column, so this needs either a ledger `kind` (additive) or careful description matching | M | Proposed — add `WalletTransaction.kind` at write sites first; matching descriptions after the fact is fragile |
| 8 | **Node cost completeness nudge** — Products tab already refuses to show a margin for a node with no `monthlyCostCents`; add a one-click link to set it | Medium: margins are only as good as the cost data | XS | Proposed |
| 9 | **Crawl-budget actions** — per-bot robots.txt suggestions (e.g. throttle Amazonbot, which is ~10× Googlebot's volume) and a "search errors" → redirect-map export | Medium for SEO with 65k static pages | S | Proposed — coordinate with the SEO agent (robots.txt is theirs) |
| 10 | **Cohort revenue retention (NRR)** — MRR retained per first-paid-month cohort | Medium; needs per-server price history (only current price is known) — real only once InsightsSnapshot accumulates per-user MRR | M | Proposed — extend the daily snapshot with per-customer MRR, then compute from history |
| 11 | **Signup-to-deploy drop-off by wizard step** joined to the bot-free funnel | Medium; `/admin/deploy-funnel` already has the step data | S | Proposed — link the two pages rather than duplicate |
| 12 | Forecast models fancier than linear (seasonality, Holt-Winters) | Low at this volume — a few hundred customers is not enough signal; would add false precision | M | **Rejected for now** |
| 13 | Per-visitor session replay / heatmaps | Low, privacy cost, consent burden | L | **Rejected** |

## Notes on the implemented three

- **No notification channel yet.** Alerts are surfaced on `/admin/insights` (Overview) only. The
  node-capacity monitor (`worker/monitor.ts`) already emails reports@ for live utilisation; these
  forecast alerts are deliberately page-only until the owner chooses a channel (item 6), to avoid a
  second source of capacity email.
- **Dismissal is sticky** per `dedupeKey` (`capacity:<nodeId>`, `rev_drop:<day>` …): a dismissed
  alert never re-opens for the same condition; a capacity alert that clears is auto-RESOLVED.
- **The churn-risk score is a ranking, not a probability.** Weights are stated in code and in the
  UI ("signals"); nothing automated happens to a flagged customer.

## Data model reference

From `/opt/nxeon/prisma/schema.prisma` — 60 models, 13 enums. `Job` is the spine: every VM mutation is
a row in it.

**Enums.**

| Enum | Line | Values |
|---|---|---|
| `Role` | `:10` | `CUSTOMER` `SUPPORT` `BILLING` `ADMIN` |
| `ServerStatus` | `:17` | `PENDING` `PROVISIONING` `RUNNING` `STOPPED` `SUSPENDED` `REINSTALLING` `DELETING` `ERROR` |
| `JobStatus` | `:28` | `QUEUED` `RUNNING` `DONE` `FAILED` |
| `JobType` | `:35` | 35 values — see the Job-lifecycle chapter |
| `TicketStatus` | `:73` | `OPEN` `ANSWERED` `CUSTOMER_REPLY` `CLOSED` |
| `TicketPriority` | `:80` | `LOW` `NORMAL` `HIGH` `URGENT` |

## Environment variables and feature flags

`BotIpFlag` (expiring honeypot/velocity flags), `CrawlerIpVerdict`, `CrawlerDaily`, `CrawlerUrl`,
`CrawlLogCursor`, `InsightsSnapshot`, `InsightsAlert`.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

## A3 insights: report (stopped early because of the usage pause; not finished)

**Branch:** `feature/admin-insights-and-bot-filter` · **Worktree:** `/opt/nxeon-wt-insights`
**Commits:** `52be77803a` (bot filtering), `a023ee85f5` (admin insights). Both pushed by the hook. Progress note is at `/root/agent-notes/insights.md`.

### Two things were never checked. Do these before merging
1. **The final typecheck never ran.** The heavy-lock queue was more than 20 deep. One run timed out on the lock and one was cancelled when the pause message arrived. An earlier run exited 0 with no output, but it may have started before the later files existed. Run: `heavy.sh bash -c "cd /opt/nxeon-wt-insights && npx tsc --noEmit -p ."`
2. **No dev-server or Playwright render.** `/admin/insights` has never been rendered in a browser. The verify script was written but cancelled before it ran. The throwaway DB `nxeon_agt_insights` and its role `agt_insights` still exist, as does the worktree `.env`. Drop all three after verifying.

### Why this was needed
Read-only checks of prod showed 44% of `Visit` rows were bots:
- **Lightpanda/1.0**, a headless browser: about 3k rows a day from residential-proxy IPs.
- **A stale-browser fleet**: Chrome 118-121 and Firefox 120-121 strings rotated across hundreds of IPs.

Run against prod's UA counts, the classifier marks about 21k of 48k rows as bots.

### What changed
**Bot classification and filtering**
- **Classifier (`lib/bots/*`):**
  - Named catalogue of about 70 crawlers, plus automation and HTTP-library patterns.
  - Official crawler IP lists and datacenter ranges, committed as a generated JSON file.
  - Reverse-DNS verification with a cached result per IP.
  - Checks for very old browser builds and iOS 13 or older.
  - A parser for the nginx access log.
  - A signed-in account is never flagged on weak signals or shared-IP flags.
- **Schema (all additive):**
  - New `Visit` columns: `isBot`, `botKind`, `botReason`, `botCheckedAt`, `interacted`, `webdriver`, plus an `(isBot, createdAt)` index.
  - New models: `BotIpFlag`, `CrawlerIpVerdict`, `CrawlerDaily`, `CrawlerUrl`, `CrawlLogCursor`, `InsightsSnapshot`, `InsightsAlert`.
- **Ingest:**
  - `/api/track` now classifies and stores bots instead of dropping them.
  - `VisitTracker` sends a webdriver flag and an interaction flag.
  - It also renders a hidden honeypot link to `/api/track/hp`, which is disallowed in robots.txt.
- **Worker:**
  - A re-classifier (bursts of requests, page sweeps, UA clusters, DNS checks).
  - An access-log crawler sweep that survives log rotation.
  - Both run on their own timers. They are not awaited, so they cannot delay the job loop.
- **Analytics:** every visitor read now excludes bots, including retention/win-back, acquisition attribution and Google Ads conversions. An audited admin cookie toggle can include them again.

**`/admin/insights`**
- 10 tabs:
  - revenue/MRR/ARR
  - churn, cohorts, LTV and a churn-risk list
  - the bot-free funnel with time to first deploy and conversion by source, partner and country
  - free-Minecraft to paid
  - margin by product
  - node capacity forecast
  - jobs and support
  - partners and email
  - payments and refunds
  - bots and crawlers
- Every tab has a date range, comparison with the previous period, and an audited CSV export.
- It says "not enough data" where the numbers are missing.
- Proposals are in `docs/ADMIN-INSIGHTS-PROPOSALS.md`. The top 3 are built: capacity forecast alerts, revenue/payment anomaly alerts (both shown on the page only, no email), and the churn-risk list.

### How it was verified
- Unit tests: `test/bot-classify.test.ts` (14 pass, using real UA strings from our own logs) and `test/insights-stats.test.ts` (6 pass).
- On the throwaway DB, filled by `scripts/seed-insights-sandbox.ts` (it refuses to run on a non-scratch DB):
  - the backfill (dry run, real run, and an idempotent re-run)
  - all worker sweeps
  - log-rotation handling
- EXPLAIN ANALYZE at 300k synthetic rows: every query under 220 ms.

### Owner actions after deploy (prod writes I did not run)
1. `cd /opt/nxeon && npx tsx scripts/backfill-bot-classification.ts --dry-run`, then run it without `--dry-run`.
2. Optional crawler history from rotated logs: `npx tsx scripts/backfill-crawler-log.ts --dry-run`, then without.
3. Quarterly: `npx tsx scripts/refresh-datacenter-ranges.ts`, then commit the JSON.

### Files edited outside my area
- `worker/index.ts` (one import, one line)
- `lib/admin-groups.ts` (one nav tab)
- `lib/rbac.ts` (one route entry)
- `lib/google-ads.ts`, `lib/retention.ts`, `lib/user-attribution.ts`, `components/admin/GoogleAdsClicksPanel.tsx` (bot filters only)

### Risks and gaps
- MRR history only starts from the first daily snapshot after deploy.
- Job queue wait and run time can't be separated until D1 adds `Job.startedAt`/`finishedAt`. The code detects them automatically when they appear.
- Chargebacks only show if an admin records them; there is no Stripe dispute webhook.
- The honeypot link is in a shared tracker component, so it renders on every page.
- About 640 KB of datacenter-range JSON is bundled into the server.
- I did not run the seed scripts that wrote `/root/nxeon-credentials.txt`.
